t: 2174. Remove All Ones With Row and Column Flips II
o: Each operation picks a cell that currently holds a 1 and zeroes its entire row and column. With m*n <= 15, encode the whole grid as a bitmask of at most 15 bits and search over states: from a state, every set bit (i, j) is a legal operation whose result is mask minus row i's bits minus column j's bits. BFS over the (at most 2^15) states gives the minimum number of operations. Example 1: clearing row/col of (1,1) then (0,0) finishes in 2, matching the BFS optimum.
k: State space is tiny: grids fit in a 15-bit mask, so BFS/DP over masks is exhaustive and exact.
An operation on any currently-set cell is always legal; its effect is mask &= ~(rowMask[i] | colMask[j]).

a.i: Treat each reachable grid as a node; edges are the legal operations. BFS from the initial mask to the empty mask yields the shortest operation sequence.
s: Precompute rowMask[i] and colMask[j] as bitmasks over cell index i*n+j.
BFS from the initial mask; expand by every set bit, applying the row/column clear.
Return the distance at which mask 0 is reached.
a.t: O(2^(mn) * mn) — each of up to 2^15 states expands over its set bits

a.i: The same state graph explored recursively with caching: dfs(mask) = 1 + min over set bits of dfs(after clearing), which is equivalent to BFS but often shorter to write.
s: Precompute row/column masks as in Approach 1.
dfs(0) = 0; dfs(mask) tries every set bit and takes 1 + the best recursive result.
Memoize on mask and return dfs(initial).
a.t: O(2^(mn) * mn) — each mask solved once, scanning its set bits
a.sp: O(2^(mn)) memo plus recursion depth up to 15

w: Both searches are exact; BFS avoids deep recursion, DFS memoization is terser. Pitfall: the operation requires grid[i][j] == 1 at execution time — restricting expansion to currently set bits handles this automatically. Note the answer never exceeds the number of 1-cells. Follow-up: version I of this problem (unlimited-cost flips) has a greedy row/column solution — contrast why that fails here.
